query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In the as-solidified Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy, grain boundaries serve as the primary mediators for dynamic deformation by acting as preferential sites for dislocation nucleation and subsequent dislocation entanglement, such that under low temperature/strain‐rate conditions the deformation is governed by thermally activated nucleation from GBs leading to moderate flow stresses, while at high strain rates (and/or elevated temperatures) increased viscous drag and enhanced dislocation entanglement at GBs lead to a higher strain rate sensitivity and elevated yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: As-solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy exhibiting a polycrystalline FCC microstructure with typical grain boundary distributions.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled variations in temperature and strain rate in atomistic simulations to mimic tension and compression tests.
generation.conditions: Simulated mechanical loading at low versus high strain rates and at varying temperatures (e.g., near room temperature versus elevated temperatures) while maintaining the as-solidified microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries that nucleate dislocations and facilitate their entanglement, leading to stacking fault formation and dislocation interactions.
generation.mechanism: Under dynamic loading, the grain boundaries lower the activation barrier for dislocation nucleation. At lower strain rates and temperatures, thermally activated dislocation motion governs plasticity, while at higher strain rates and temperatures, the combination of insufficient time for dislocations to overcome energy barriers and the increased phonon drag fosters greater dislocation entanglement, thereby increasing yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Simulations will show that at low temperature and strain rate, dislocation nucleation occurs primarily via thermally activated processes from GBs with moderate stress response, whereas at high strain rates and/or elevated temperatures, there is a marked increase in dislocation entanglement at GBs, resulting in a higher yield strength and greater strain rate sensitivity.
generation.baseline: The dynamic response of similar Co-containing HEAs, where stacking fault mediated dislocation dynamics contribute to the strength–ductility balance, provides a comparative baseline.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to as-solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn alloys with typical polycrystalline microstructures; deviations are expected if the microstructure is heavily deformed or thermally annealed, significantly altering the grain boundary character.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative changes in yield strength and strain rate sensitivity, as well as the relative contributions of dislocation nucleation versus phonon drag effects, remain uncertain until simulation parameters are fully explored.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of controlled atomistic simulations of the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy under tensile and compressive loading at varying temperatures (e.g., 300 K and higher) and strain rates (ranging from 10^−3 s^−1 to 10^3 s^−1). Compare the initiation sites of dislocation nucleation, measure dislocation densities, stacking fault fractions, and yield strength evolution. Two sets of simulations should be run: one with a focus on grain boundary engineering (typical GB distributions) and one with artificially suppressed GB contributions.
measurements: Onset strain for dislocation nucleation at grain boundaries
Dislocation density and entanglement metrics as a function of strain
Stacking fault atom fraction over deformation
Flow stress and yield strength from stress–strain curves
Strain rate sensitivity of mechanical response
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simulation results show no significant difference in dislocation nucleation or entanglement attributable to grain boundaries across the tested temperature and strain rate regimes—i.e., if the yield strength and flow stress curves do not vary as predicted (with enhanced strain rate sensitivity and increased dislocation entanglement at high strain rates/temperatures) compared to the control simulation—then the hypothesis that GB-mediated dislocation dynamics govern the dynamic response of solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: At 300 K, stress in CoNiCrFeMn HEA NW reaches up to 5.5 GPa at around 5% strain, as shown in Figure 2b during elastic deformation. Multiple partial dislocations nucleate simultaneously at different slip planes across NW as can be seen in Figure 5b. It has been thought that HEAs own the lattice distortion effect which will be amplified under higher temperatures. Therefore, the activation barriers of dislocation nucleation could be lower than those at 77 K, which gives rise to more partial dislocation nucleation at different sites. Subsequently, on further loading, more partial dislocations nucleate and glide through the NW, inducing the deformation twinning and martensitic transformation to the HCP phase. Interestingly, the reorientation mechanism can still exist and contribute to the extended plasticity until the fracture of NW caused by necking as shown in Figure 5b. Overall, the exceptional strength-ductility trade-off of HEA NW at low temperature is a synergistic result of operative mechanisms involving the twinning, phase transformation, and also the re-orientation of the NW cross-section. Compressive yield strength was calculated at 5% strain and plotted on a double-logarithmic scale of flow stress (MPa) versus strain rate (s−1) as shown in Fig. 3c. SRS of two different regimes was obtained from the slope of a linear fit as shown by the dotted lines. The SRS was 0.03 for low strain rates (10–3 s−1–10–1 s−1) while it was about an order of magnitude higher with a value of 0.2 in the high strain rate (102 s−1–103 s−1) regime. At low strain rates, dislocation velocities are small and that leads to negligible effect of phonon drag on dislocation motion. Therefore, flow stress changes at a slower rate with change in strain rate and mostly depends on thermally activated dislocation glide. The SRS value of our alloy is larger compared to other single-phase FCC HEAs reported in literature, such as Al0.1CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeMnNi. The high SRS value at high strain rates may be attributed to two factors: (i) not enough time for thermally activated dislocations to cross the energy barrier and (ii) strong effect of viscous phonon drag on dislocation motion.
